1251.quote_or_event: “Behold, O Siblings of Destiny, the storm of spiritual wisdom has come. It has totally blown away the thatched huts of doubt, and torn apart the bonds of Maya.”
1251.explanation: Kabir describes an overwhelming inner force that sweeps away the flimsy shelter the mind had built around itself.
1251.tie_back: The Kural pictures love as an axe smashing the door of reserve bolted with modesty; Kabir likewise pictures a force too strong for the mind's defences, which simply tears the old structure down.
1251.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 331, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1251._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of a defence broken by a greater force, but what Kabir's storm destroys is doubt and Maya, not modesty, and the power is spiritual wisdom rather than love-longing.

1252.quote_or_event: “I am thirsty, thirsty for the Lord; the soul-bride gazes upon Him all through the night.”
1252.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a bride so possessed by longing that she keeps watch the whole night instead of sleeping.
1252.tie_back: The Kural's wife complains that love is a pitiless master that rules her heart even at midnight when everyone else rests; Guru Nanak's bride is likewise kept awake all night by her thirst for the Beloved.
1252.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1232, Raag Saarang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1252._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on longing that rules the night, though Gurbani does not call this love cruel, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1253.quote_or_event: “Now the moon emerged in the sky of heart cannot remain hidden in spite of efforts to cover its light with flour kneading basin.”
1253.explanation: In a stanza describing the delight of those drenched in love, Bhai Gurdas says such love shows itself however hard one tries to cover it, like moonlight under an upturned bowl.
1253.tie_back: The Kural's wife says she tries to hide her love but it bursts out without warning like a sneeze; Bhai Gurdas likewise says love that has risen in the heart cannot be kept covered.
1253.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 13, Pauri 6 (English translation as given on BaniDB)
1253._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Vaar 13, Pauri 6); strong thematic fit on love that cannot be concealed, but this is early Sikh exegesis rather than scripture, and the love meant is devotion to God and the Guru, not romantic love.

1254.quote_or_event: “My shyness and hesitation have died and gone, and I walk with my face unveiled.”
1254.explanation: Guru Nanak speaks as a soul-bride whose fear of what people will say has vanished, so that she now goes about openly, without her veil.
1254.tie_back: The Kural's wife admits that the reserve she once claimed is gone and her love now shows in the public square; Guru Nanak's bride likewise has shed her shyness and walks unveiled before everyone.
1254.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 931, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1254._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on modesty overcome and love made public, though Gurbani treats the loss of worldly shyness as freedom while the Kural's heroine feels it as defeat, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1255.quote_or_event: “Cutting off my head, I give it to Him to sit upon; without my head, I shall still serve Him.”
1255.explanation: Guru Nanak's soul-bride is ready to give up even her head, the seat of pride, to serve the one who brings her news of the Beloved.
1255.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that those sick with love do not know the dignity of refusing to follow one who has turned away; Guru Nanak's bride likewise sets all self-regard aside for the sake of her Beloved.
1255.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 558, Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1255._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit on love that abandons pride, though Gurbani praises this surrender while the Kural voices it as a helpless loss of dignity, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1256.quote_or_event: “My mind and body are so thirsty for the Blessed Vision of His Darshan. Won't someone please come and lead me to him, O my mother.”
1256.explanation: In his Barah Maha, Guru Arjan describes a longing so strong that the bride begs anyone at all to take her to her Beloved.
1256.tie_back: The Kural's wife marvels at the grief that makes her long to follow the very one who left her; Guru Arjan's bride is likewise driven by her ache to seek out the absent Beloved.
1256.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1256._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on grief that drives the lover to follow, though Gurbani never treats the Lord as one who has scorned the bride, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1257.quote_or_event: “She surrenders her body and mind to Him, and does not remain separate from Him.”
1257.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas describes the beloved bride who holds nothing back from her Husband and keeps no distance from Him.
1257.tie_back: The Kural's wife says that when her beloved lovingly does what she desires she no longer knows anything called shyness; Ravidas's bride likewise keeps no reserve at all before the Husband she loves.
1257.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 793, Raag Soohee, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1257._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit on reserve that vanishes in love, though Ravidas means complete self-surrender to God rather than the end of a wife's shyness, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1258.quote_or_event: “So listen, O my sisters - the Enticer has enticed my mind. My body and mind are drenched with Nectar.”
1258.explanation: Guru Nanak's bride tells her companions that the Beloved, the Enticer, has won her mind completely.
1258.tie_back: The Kural's wife calls her beloved a thief of many wiles whose coaxing words broke down her womanly firmness; Guru Nanak's bride likewise confesses to her friends that the Enticer has captured her mind.
1258.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 764, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1258._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on a fondly named beloved who wins the heart, but Gurbani has no image of coaxing words as an army breaking a fortress, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1259.quote_or_event: “The bride may be hunch-backed and short, but if she is loved by her Lord Master, she becomes beautiful, and she melts in the Lord's embrace.”
1259.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that whatever the bride's flaws, once her Lord loves her she melts into His embrace.
1259.tie_back: The Kural's wife went meaning to sulk but, seeing her heart already rushing to him, embraced him instead; Guru Ram Das's bride likewise melts into her Lord's embrace.
1259.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 527, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1259._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of melting into the embrace, but has no planned sulk that gives way, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.

1260.quote_or_event: “As metal melts into metal again, so does love melt into love.”
1260.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the image of molten metal flowing into metal to show how love naturally merges with the one it loves.
1260.tie_back: The Kural asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in the fire could ever hold firm in a sulk once they are together; Guru Nanak likewise pictures love as something that melts and merges on contact.
1260.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 725, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1260._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on the melting image and the impossibility of holding apart, though Guru Nanak speaks of the soul's love merging with God, and the love meant is spiritual, not romantic.
